passage:
Monday. Pradeep didn't get into the school band. He said, "It's fine," but his ears were red. Siddharth answered, "It's not a big deal, there's always next year." Pradeep looked away and said, "Yeah, right," and left early.

Wednesday. Siddharth couldn't stop thinking about Pradeep's face. He messaged, "That came out like your thing didn't matter. Sorry. Want to talk, or want me to just sit with you?" Pradeep replied, "Sit."

Saturday. They sat on the steps outside the music room. Pradeep talked about how much he'd practised. Siddharth said only, "That sounds really disappointing," and stayed. Pradeep leaned on the railing, breathing slowly, and finally said, "Thanks for staying."

qa.q: What did Pradeep not get into?
qa.a: He did not get into the school band.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep say "Yeah, right" and leave early on Monday?
qa.a: He was probably hurt and felt his disappointment was being brushed aside, since his ears were red and he looked away. He may also just have wanted to be alone.

qa.q: What worked better for Siddharth on Saturday than on Monday?
qa.a: Instead of offering a quick fix or calling it small, he listened, named the disappointment and stayed with Pradeep.

qa.q: How might Siddharth have felt after Pradeep left early?
qa.a: He may have felt worried and unsure, which is why he messaged to apologise on Wednesday.

grounding: A teenager comforts a friend by listening and staying, after minimising did not help.

passage: My grandson Hrithik asked me how to help a friend who was upset, so I told him about my school friend Tejas. I was your age then, Hrithik, and Tejas failed his board mathematics paper. I said all the clever things: "It's only one paper. You'll pass the supplementary." Tejas's jaw went hard and he stopped speaking to me for two days. I had answered the problem, not the person. So I went to his house with a small packet of jalebis and said, "I'm sorry. I'm here. You don't have to say anything." We sat on his verandah for an hour. He talked a little. Sometimes that's all it takes, just showing up and listening.

qa.q: What did Tejas fail?
qa.a: He failed his board mathematics paper.

qa.q: Why did Tejas stop speaking to his friend for two days?
qa.a: He felt brushed aside by clever comments, since his jaw went hard after hearing that it was only one paper. He probably wanted to feel understood first.

qa.q: What did the narrator change on the second visit?
qa.a: The narrator apologised, stayed with Tejas and did not push him to talk, which let Tejas open up a little.

qa.q: How might the narrator have felt on seeing Tejas's jaw go hard?
qa.a: The narrator probably came to feel regretful, seeing that the clever words answered the problem and not the person, which is why they went to apologise with jalebis.

grounding: An elder recalls that fixing or minimising felt dismissive to a friend, and listening and presence helped.

passage:
Afreen had exactly five minutes between chemistry and maths, and the corridor was packed. She found Kiran by the lockers, staring at the notice board. The state team list. Kiran's name wasn't on it.
"Hey," Afreen said. "It's not a big deal, there's always next year."
Kiran's jaw tightened. "Right. Sure."
Afreen saw it immediately, the flat voice, the way Kiran turned back to the lockers. She stopped herself.
"Sorry. That came out wrong. It is a big deal. You trained all year."
Kiran's eyes filled. "I was so sure this time."
The bell rang. Afreen didn't move for a moment. "I have to go, but I'm here at lunch. Same bench. You don't have to talk."
In maths she sent a message under the desk: "Proud of you for trying. Lunch, bench, I'll bring the chips."
At lunch Kiran was already there.

qa.q: How many minutes did Afreen have between chemistry and maths?
qa.a: She had exactly five minutes.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling after Afreen said it wasn't a big deal?
qa.a: Kiran felt hurt and resentful, shown by the tight jaw and flat "Right. Sure," because the loss had been brushed aside.

qa.q: What went wrong first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Minimising the loss felt dismissive; Afreen fixed it by apologising, saying it was a big deal, and offering to simply be there at lunch.

qa.q: What would change if Afreen had kept trying to cheer Kiran up with next year?
qa.a: Kiran would probably have shut down further and felt less understood, and might not have come to the bench at lunch.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager comforting a friend, first minimising the loss, then validating it and staying present.

passage:
On the stairs of their building in Kochi, Jomon found Minakshi sitting between the third and fourth floors, knees up, phone dark in her hand.
"Minakshi? You okay?"
She shrugged. "My parents are separating. They told me at lunch."
Jomon sat down two steps below her. He wanted to say something wise. He had nothing. So he said, "That's really hard."
She nodded. For a long time neither of them said anything. A neighbour's pressure cooker whistled somewhere. Jomon didn't check his phone.
"I keep thinking it's because they fought about my fees," she said finally.
"That sounds heavy to carry."
She wiped her face. "You're not telling me it'll be fine."
"I don't know if it will. I'm just here."
Later that night he sent her one line: "Still here if you want the stairs tomorrow." She replied with a single heart.

qa.q: Where did Jomon find Minakshi?
qa.a: He found her on the stairs between the third and fourth floors.

qa.q: What did Minakshi's words "You're not telling me it'll be fine" suggest she felt?
qa.a: They suggest she felt relieved and understood that Jomon wasn't brushing her sadness aside with easy promises.

qa.q: What made Jomon's support work?
qa.a: He listened, stayed present without his phone, named how hard it was, and sent a short message later instead of trying to fix the situation.

qa.q: What is it like for Minakshi to think the separation was about her fees?
qa.a: It seems to make her feel guilty and heavy, as if she were partly to blame, which is why being heard mattered so much.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager comforting a friend by listening, staying present and sending a supportive message rather than fixing.

passage:
"She's gone, Jomon. Zara left for Canada this morning."
"Parveen, okay, but you can video call every day! And there are apps where you watch films together. And she'll be back in summer, probably."
Parveen stared at him. "I didn't ask for a plan."
"I'm just trying to help."
"You're trying to make it not sad. It is sad."
Jomon opened his mouth to argue, then closed it. He put the phone with the app list back in his pocket.
"You're right. Sorry. Tell me about this morning."
Parveen's shoulders dropped. "She gave me her old jacket at the airport. And I just stood there till the car left."
"That sounds awful. You've been friends since Class 2."
"Since Class 1."
"Since Class 1," he repeated, and she almost smiled.

qa.q: What did Zara give Parveen at the airport?
qa.a: She gave Parveen her old jacket at the airport.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when she said "I didn't ask for a plan"?
qa.a: She was sad and a little resentful, feeling that Jomon's quick solutions were brushing her grief aside.

qa.q: What could Jomon try first next time a friend is upset?
qa.a: Ask them to tell what happened and listen, like he did after apologising, before offering any fixes.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt when Parveen pushed back?
qa.a: He probably felt stung and a bit defensive, since he was trying to help, before realising she needed listening, not a plan.

grounding: The dialogue shows a friend first fixing and minimising, then switching to listening and validation, which the friend needed more.

passage: Last month Keerthana found out she hadn't made the state volleyball squad, and I said exactly the wrong thing first. We were sitting on the steps behind the court and she was ripping a leaf into tiny strips. I said, "Hey, it's not a big deal, there's always next year. You could work on your serve." She went completely still. "Thanks, Lalit. Very helpful," she said, flat as a wall, and got up. I felt stupid. That night I didn't send tips. I wrote: "Sorry about earlier. I know how much you wanted this. I'm not going to fix it. I'm just around if you want to rant." She called twenty minutes later and talked for almost an hour, mostly about her coach and how unfair the trial felt. I said maybe ten sentences. At the end she said, "That helped." I still don't know what I said. I think that was the point.

qa.q: Where were they sitting when Lalit said the wrong thing?
qa.a: They were sitting on the steps behind the court.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel after Keerthana walked away?
qa.a: Lalit felt stupid and probably guilty for shrinking the disappointment, which is why the night message apologised and offered listening instead of tips.

qa.q: What changed between the first reply and the night message?
qa.a: Lalit stopped fixing and minimising, named how much Keerthana wanted it, apologised and offered to listen, which let her talk for almost an hour.

qa.q: What was it like for Keerthana to hear 'it's not a big deal'?
qa.a: It made Keerthana feel her disappointment was brushed aside, so she went still, answered flatly and left.

grounding: It shows a teenager learning that minimising and quick fixes feel dismissive, while listening and a supportive message help someone who is hurting.
